One cloud Mac per developer, or several projects on one Mac?

Reviewed: 2026-11-21 · WodeMac

When everyone builds, tests or runs simulators every day, one dedicated cloud Mac per developer is simplest: environments, permissions and disks stay separate and nobody's build slows down anyone else. For a small team with light projects that can take turns, one Mac can host several projects: give each branch its own directory with git worktree, keep each task in tmux, and watch the 16GB memory and 256GB storage limits. Start with one Mac, then add machines per person or per project.

One each, or one shared: how to choose

  • One Mac per developer when everyone runs Xcode builds, tests or simulators daily; projects need conflicting dependency versions; each person manages their own accounts and credentials; you want a clear record of who changed what.
  • One shared Mac when the team is small, the work is mostly scripts, web or backend projects, builds are occasional and can be staggered, and one person maintains the setup.

The remote screen shows one desktop, so two people using it at the same time get in each other's way. On a shared Mac, agree who uses the desktop when, and keep everyone else's work in terminals and background jobs.

Parallel branches on one Mac: git worktree

Switching branches in one directory interrupts running builds and mixes up uncommitted changes. A git worktree checks out a branch in its own directory while sharing the repository history:

git worktree add ../myapp-feature-a -b feature-a
git worktree add ../myapp-hotfix -b hotfix-login
git worktree list
git worktree remove ../myapp-feature-a   # clean up after merging

Each worktree is a fresh checkout, so install dependencies in it, and copy gitignored files such as .env yourself. Merge through reviewed pull requests and remove worktrees you no longer need.

Sessions and resources: tmux, memory, disk

Give each project or branch its own tmux session (tmux new -s feature-a). It keeps running when the remote connection drops; reattach with tmux attach.

What uses resources is builds, tests and simulators running at the same time. Several xcodebuild runs at once put 16GB of memory under pressure, so start with two in parallel and check memory pressure in Activity Monitor. The 256GB disk has to hold Xcode, simulator runtimes and the dependencies of every worktree:

df -h
du -sh ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData

DerivedData is safe to delete; the next build recreates it.

Keeping several Macs consistent

Each physical Mac mini is rented to one customer; a team, as one customer, can order several and manage them together. Write the setup down so every machine matches:

brew bundle dump            # export a Brewfile from a configured Mac
brew bundle install         # install the same tools on a new Mac

Keep the required Xcode version, Git settings and project setup scripts in the repository, and push all code to a remote Git repository rather than leaving it on one machine. Each developer keeps their own accounts and credentials out of shared scripts.

FAQ

Can two people use one cloud Mac at the same time?

The remote screen shows a single desktop, so two people working on it at once get in each other's way. Take turns, or keep the second person's work in terminals and background jobs; for long-term parallel work, one Mac each is better.

How many projects can one Mac mini run at once?

There is no fixed number. The usual limits are memory used by builds, tests and simulators running together, and the 256GB disk. Start with two and check Activity Monitor and free space.

Is there a discount for teams?

Yearly orders of 5 or more Macs get 2.5% off the first year; renewals are at the yearly price.

How do we set up a new developer quickly?

List your Homebrew tools in a Brewfile and run brew bundle install, and keep the Xcode version requirement and project setup scripts in the repository so every new Mac follows the same steps.
